original_value: The monitoring and quantification of soil carbon provide a better understanding of soil and atmosphere dynamics. Visible-near-infrared-short-wave infrared (VIS-NIR-SWIR) reflectance spectroscopy can quantitatively estimate soil carbon content more rapidly and cost-effectively compared to traditional laboratory analysis. However, effective estimation of soil carbon using reflectance spectroscopy to a great extent depends on the selection of a suitable preprocessing sequence and data-mining algorithm. Many efforts have been dedicated to the comparison of conventional chemometric techniques and their optimization for soil properties prediction. Instead, the current study focuses on the potential of the new data-mining engine PARACUDA-II®, recently developed at Tel-Aviv University (TAU), by comparing its performance in predicting soil oxidizable carbon (Cox) against common data-mining algorithms including partial least squares regression (PLSR), random forests (RF), boosted regression trees (BRT), support vector machine regression (SVMR), and memory based learning (MBL). To this end, 103 soil samples from the Pokrok dumpsite in the Czech Republic were scanned with an ASD FieldSpec III Pro FR spectroradiometer in the laboratory under a strict protocol. Spectra preprocessing for conventional data-mining techniques was conducted using Savitzky-Golay smoothing and the first derivative method. PARACUDA-II®, on the other hand, operates based on the all possibilities approach (APA) concept, a conditional Latin hypercube sampling (cLHs) algorithm and parallel programming, to evaluate all of the potential combinations of eight different spectral preprocessing techniques against the original reflectance and chemical data prior to the model development. The comparison of results was made in terms of the coefficient of determination (R2) and root-mean-square error of prediction (RMSEp). Results showed that the PARACUDA-II® engine performed better than the other selected regular schemes with R2 value of 0.80 and RMSEp of 0.12; the PLSR was less predictive compared to other techniques with R2 = 0.63 and RMSEp = 0.29. This can be attributed to its capability to assess all the available options in an automatic way, which enables the hidden models to rise up and yield the best available model.

result.paraphrase: Monitoring and quantifying soil carbon helps improve understanding of soil-atmosphere dynamics. Compared with conventional laboratory analysis, visible-near-infrared-short-wave infrared (VIS-NIR-SWIR) reflectance spectroscopy can estimate soil carbon content more quickly and at lower cost. However, accurate estimation of soil carbon from reflectance spectroscopy depends largely on choosing an appropriate preprocessing sequence and data-mining algorithm. While many studies have compared standard chemometric methods and their optimization for predicting soil properties, this study instead examines the potential of the newly developed PARACUDA-II® data-mining engine from Tel-Aviv University (TAU) by testing its ability to predict soil oxidizable carbon (Cox) against widely used algorithms such as partial least squares regression (PLSR), random forests (RF), boosted regression trees (BRT), support vector machine regression (SVMR), and memory based learning (MBL). For this purpose, 103 soil samples from the Pokrok dumpsite in the Czech Republic were scanned in the laboratory using an ASD FieldSpec III Pro FR spectroradiometer under a strict protocol. For conventional data-mining methods, spectral preprocessing used Savitzky-Golay smoothing and the first derivative method. PARACUDA-II®, by contrast, uses the all possibilities approach (APA), a conditional Latin hypercube sampling (cLHs) algorithm, and parallel programming to evaluate every possible combination of eight spectral preprocessing techniques against the original reflectance and chemical data before model development. The comparison was based on the coefficient of determination (R2) and root-mean-square error of prediction (RMSEp). The results indicated that PARACUDA-II® outperformed the other selected standard schemes, achieving R2 = 0.80 and RMSEp = 0.12, whereas PLSR was the least predictive of the methods tested, with R2 = 0.63 and RMSEp = 0.29. This is likely due to its ability to automatically assess all available options, allowing hidden models to emerge and produce the best attainable model.
